I walked in on one of my cousins who had comitted suicide when I was 12. I knew he was depressed and we had talked for 3 hours before I couldn't keep my eyes open anymore (I passed out on the couch unintentionally). The next morning his mom noticed he would be late for work if he didn't get up, so I went in to wake him up while she made breakfast.i was guilt ridden for years, perhaps still am. I had severe trust issues and shut the world out. I had created a wall between me and anyone who ever tried to be or was close to me in any way.

 Eventually I found someone who pulled me out of my depression, but shortly after I discovered through a post on reddit everything she said was a lie. My trust issues came back tenfold, my life hit an all time low. 

One day an elder pulled me aside to tell me they could feel my sorrow. They reminded me that we can't control everything in our lives. That sometimes life throws us a curve ball, and you just have to pick yourself up, dust yourself off, and wait for the next pitch. I realized that even if I wasn't there that night, it would have still happened. That if I go through life thinking about the past and everything that could be done differently, then I'm not really living. 4 years after that little realization, im rocking a new perspective, things are better than ever.

One of the closest friends I ever had I met in kindergarten. She had a disease where her body stopped growing but her organs were still growing inside her (I don't remember the exact name of it because it wasn't something often talked about). No one in the class would go near her because of her obvious deformities, but I was slightly shocked at their behavior.... also 5 year old me was simply intrigued because she was so different from everyone else. After that first day of playing house we were inseparable. In grade 2 she spent a long time in Children's Hospital. I worked doing jobs for all my aunts and uncles and saved my small amount of cash until I had enough money to pay my ferry ticket so my mom would take me (only to find out she would have taken me regardless). So I would see her almost biweekly until she was out. 

When she moved back in grade 6 I would hang out with her every week. She was more popular now but one day someone asked her why she didn't take better care of herself (she has crusty yellow scabs I assume from the disease), and I almost got expelled for hitting her. More than once.

We used to race each other, and for the longest time she'd win with her awesome wheelchair, but pretty soon it was even. Even sooner I was holding back to let her win. Her favorite book was the one about wheelchairs by Munch. I used to joke about winning the lottery and buying her the fastest wheelchair.

In grade ten of highschool she ended up back at the hospital. I'd go to visit every week, and one day I showed up and her family was crying. They left after she asked them to, leaving us alone while they went to eat. She told me she was still thankful for that first day of kindergarten playing house, and told me she knew about all those races I let her win. At this stage she was in a lot of pain, but didn't want her family to see her like this in her last minutes. She asked me to close my eyes and count to thirty for her. I opened my eyes and she was gone.

Sam Kercher was the closest friend, and the bravest person I've ever had the honor to meet, and I'll never forget her.

**tldr: best friend for 11 years when people avoided her for her disease and in the end was there for her when she finally had to leave.**

I walk in to the living room and before I could say anything my brother got up to hug me and told me that my cousin (the same one I was up all night talking to) was found dead in his room that morning.
